# Pītavimānavatthu (Vv 47)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pītavimānavatthu* (Vv 47, also cited as *Pītavimāna* or Vimānavatthu 4.9) is a canonical Pali verse narrative belonging to the *Vimānavatthu* in the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral; Radich 2007]. The text depicts a dialogue in which Sakka, the king of the gods, inquires about the previous meritorious deeds of a goddess reborn in the realm of the Thirty-Three (Tāvatiṃsa) [SuttaCentral; Radich 2007; Lim Hwee San 2009]. She explains that in her previous human life at Rājagaha, she was walking to offer yellow flowers at the stupa built by King Ajātasattu for the Buddha’s relics [Radich 2007]. While engrossed in devotion towards the Teacher’s relics (*sarīra*), she failed to notice a furious rushing cow and was gored to death before she could complete her offering [Radich 2007; Lim Hwee San 2009]. Nevertheless, owing to her pure mental resolve (*cetopaṇidhihetu*), she attained an exalted heavenly rebirth [Lim Hwee San 2009].
In modern scholarship, the narrative is frequently analyzed as significant textual evidence for the early Buddhist relic cult, stupa veneration, and the decisive efficacy of mental resolve (*citta-paṇidhi* / *cetopaṇidhi*) upon death and rebirth [Radich 2007; Lim Hwee San 2009].
SuttaCentral records a curated passage-level parallel to the text in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37, *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*) [SuttaCentral]. Machine alignments generated by DharmaNexus indicate extensive Pali-internal text reuse with the commentary, the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as segments shared with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Across canonical boundaries, DharmaNexus automatically aligns passages of the text with Tibetan translations of the *Damamūko-nāma-sūtra* (D0341) and Kṣemendra's *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155-2) [DharmaNexus].
